items.stem: A consumer buying only one good is in equilibrium when
items.answer: the MU of the good in rupees equals its price
options: the MU of the good in rupees equals its price

items.stem:
Total utility (in utils) from chocolates:
Units | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
TU | 32 | 59 | 79 | 97 | 111
Find the marginal utility of unit 2.

Total utility (in utils) from oranges:
Units | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8
TU | 21 | 38 | 51 | 59 | 62 | 62 | 56 | 45
At which unit does marginal utility become zero, and what is TU there?
items.answer: Unit 6; TU = 62 utils (maximum)
items.markingKey: MU of unit 6 = 62 − 62 = 0; TU is maximum when MU = 0 and falls after that.

items.stem:
Marginal utility (in utils) from bananas:
Units | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
MU | 28 | 25 | 18 | 14 | 8 | 6
If 1 util = ₹5 and the price is ₹125 per unit, how many units will the consumer buy?
items.answer: 2 units
items.markingKey: MU in ₹ = MU × 5: 140, 125, 90, 70, 40, 30. The consumer buys while MU (₹) ≥ price; at unit 2, MU = ₹125 = price. Equilibrium: 2 units.

items.stem:
A consumer spends ₹27 on goods X and Y. Price of X = ₹3, price of Y = ₹6. Marginal utilities (utils) are:
Units | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
MU of X | 20 | 18 | 15 | 13 | 9 | 6
MU of Y | 23 | 18 | 16 | 14 | 13 | 10
Find the equilibrium combination using the law of equi-marginal utility.
items.answer: 5 units of X and 2 units of Y
items.markingKey: MUx/Px = 9/3 = 3 = MUy/Py = 18/6; spending = 3×5 + 6×2 = ₹27 = income. 2 marks ratios; 1 mark budget check; 1 mark answer.

items.stem: State and explain the law of diminishing marginal utility with a schedule.
items.answer: As more units of a good are consumed, MU from each successive unit falls; schedule showing falling MU and TU rising at a falling rate, maximum when MU = 0.
items.markingKey: 1 mark statement; 2 marks schedule and explanation.

items.stem: Explain consumer's equilibrium in the case of two commodities using the law of equi-marginal utility. What happens if MUx/Px > MUy/Py?
items.answer: Equilibrium when MUx/Px = MUy/Py = MU of a rupee and income is fully spent; if MUx/Px > MUy/Py, the consumer buys more X and less Y; MUx falls and MUy rises till ratios are equal.
items.markingKey: 2 marks conditions; 2 marks explanation; 2 marks adjustment (6 marks).

items.stem: The horizontal intercept of the budget line (good 1 on x-axis) is
items.answer: M/p₁
items.markingKey: (a) All income on good 1.

items.stem: How does the budget line change when: Both prices double; income is unchanged?
items.answer: Parallel inward shift
items.markingKey: (c) Both prices double; income is unchanged: Parallel inward shift.
options: Rotates outward; good 1 intercept moves out
No change in the budget line
Rotates inward; good 2 intercept moves in

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The slope of the budget line is −p₁/p₂.
Reason (R): It shows the rate at which the market allows good 2 to be exchanged for good 1.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Income = ₹80; price of notebooks = ₹20, price of pencils = ₹10. Where does the bundle (0 notebooks, 1 pencils) lie?
items.answer: Inside the budget set: ₹70 is left unspent
items.markingKey: (b) Cost = 20×0 + 10×1 = ₹10 against income ₹80.
options: Inside the budget set: ₹90 is left unspent
Inside the budget set: ₹70 is left unspent
On the budget line: it costs exactly ₹80

items.stem: A budget line has slope −1 and meets the books axis at 4 units. If the price of books is ₹10, find the price of movie tickets and the consumer's income.
items.answer: Price of movie tickets = ₹10; income = ₹40

items.stem:
Om has a pocket allowance of ₹70 to spend on chocolates (price ₹5) and biscuits (price ₹2).
(i) Write the equation of the budget line.
(ii) Find the maximum quantity of chocolates that can be bought.
(iii) Find the slope of the budget line.
(iv) What happens to the budget line if the allowance doubles and prices remain the same?
items.answer: (i) 5x₁ + 2x₂ = 70; (ii) 14 units; (iii) −p₁/p₂ = −5/2; (iv) Parallel outward shift (intercepts 28 and 70)
items.markingKey: 1 mark each (4 marks).

items.stem: Income rises from ₹100 to ₹1,300; prices of chocolates and biscuits stay at ₹20 and ₹20. Find the new intercepts and describe the change in the budget line.
items.answer: 65 units of chocolates and 65 units of biscuits; the line shifts parallel outward
items.markingKey: New intercepts 1300/20 = 65 and 1300/20 = 65; slope −p₁/p₂ unchanged, so a parallel shift.

items.stem: Explain the budget line. Derive its slope. Show with diagrams how it changes when (i) income rises, (ii) price of good 2 rises.
items.answer: Bundles costing exactly M; p₁x₁ + p₂x₂ = M; slope −p₁/p₂ (from intercepts M/p₁, M/p₂); (i) parallel outward shift; (ii) rotates inward along the good 2 axis, good 1 intercept unchanged.
items.markingKey: 2 marks meaning and slope; 2 marks each change (6 marks).

items.stem: A consumer has an income of ₹400 to spend on mangoes (good 1, price ₹8) and oranges (good 2, price ₹25). What is the maximum quantity of oranges the consumer can buy?
items.markingKey: Intercept = M/p = 400/25 = 16 (spending all income on oranges).

items.stem: A consumer has an income of ₹80 to spend on notebooks (good 1, price ₹20) and pencils (good 2, price ₹20). What is the maximum quantity of pencils the consumer can buy?
items.markingKey: Intercept = M/p = 80/20 = 4 (spending all income on pencils).

items.stem: At the consumer's optimum (with a convex IC), the budget line is
items.answer: tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve
items.markingKey: (b) Tangency: MRS = p₁/p₂.
options: tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve

items.stem: A consumer has monotonic preferences. Compare bundle P = (4, 2) with bundle Q = (7, 3) (units of good 1, good 2).
items.answer: Bundle Q is preferred
items.markingKey: (a) It has more of at least one good and no less of the other.
options: The consumer is indifferent between them
Cannot be decided from monotonic preferences alone

items.stem: At a bundle on her budget line, a consumer's MRS (units of good 2 she is willing to give up for one more unit of good 1) is 0.75. The prices are p₁ = ₹5 and p₂ = ₹4. What should she do to raise her satisfaction?
items.answer: Buy less of good 1 and more of good 2
items.markingKey: (b) MRS = 0.75 < p₁/p₂ = 1.25. She values good 1 less than the market does, so she buys less of good 1.
options: Buy less of good 1 and more of good 2
Stay at the same bundle: it is the optimum
Buy more of good 1 and less of good 2

items.stem:
A consumer is indifferent between these bundles of apples (good 1) and oranges (good 2):
Bundle | A | B | C | D | E
Apples | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
Oranges | 24 | 17 | 11 | 6 | 5
Find the MRS (units of oranges per unit of apples) when the consumer moves from C to D.
items.markingKey: MRS = ΔY/ΔX = 5/1 = 5. MRS falls along the curve: 7, 6, 5, 1.

items.stem: At a bundle on her budget line, a consumer's MRS (units of good 2 she is willing to give up for one more unit of good 1) is 0.38. The prices are p₁ = ₹3 and p₂ = ₹8. What should she do to raise her satisfaction?
items.answer: Stay at the same bundle: it is the optimum
items.markingKey: (a) MRS = 0.38 = p₁/p₂ = 0.38. MRS = price ratio: optimum.
options: Stay at the same bundle: it is the optimum
Buy more of good 1 and less of good 2
Buy less of good 1 and more of good 2

items.stem:
Bundles of bananas (good 1) and mangoes (good 2) giving equal satisfaction:
Bundle | A | B | C | D | E
Bananas | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
Mangoes | 25 | 17 | 11 | 7 | 5
(i) Find the MRS between A and B.
(ii) Is the MRS diminishing? What shape does this give the indifference curve?
(iii) Why is the indifference curve downward sloping?
(iv) State the condition for the consumer's optimum.
items.answer: (i) 8; (ii) Yes (8, 6, 4, 2); convex to the origin; (iii) With monotonic preferences, more of good 1 must be balanced by less of good 2 to keep satisfaction the same; (iv) MRS = p₁/p₂ at a point on the budget line (tangency), with MRS diminishing
items.markingKey: 1 mark each (4 marks).

items.stem: Explain the meaning of marginal rate of substitution with an example. Why does it diminish?
items.answer: Units of good 2 the consumer is willing to give up for one more unit of good 1; e.g. 4 mangoes for 1 banana; it diminishes because as good 1 becomes more plentiful its relative worth falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark example; 1 mark reason.

items.stem: Explain the conditions of consumer's equilibrium using indifference curve analysis. What happens if MRS > p₁/p₂?
items.answer: Budget line tangent to the highest IC: MRS = p₁/p₂ and MRS diminishing (IC convex). If MRS > p₁/p₂, the consumer values good 1 more than the market, buys more of it and less of good 2; MRS falls till equal.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each condition; 2 marks adjustment (6 marks).

items.stem: A consumer has monotonic preferences. Compare bundle P = (12, 6) with bundle Q = (10, 4) (units of good 1, good 2).
items.answer: Bundle P is preferred
items.markingKey: (a) It has more of at least one good and no less of the other.
options: Cannot be decided from monotonic preferences alone
The consumer is indifferent between them

items.stem:
Assertion (A): An indifference curve is convex to the origin.
Reason (R): The MRS diminishes as the consumer gets more of good 1.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Demand for a good with many close substitutes tends to be
items.answer: elastic
items.markingKey: (d) Easy to switch.

items.stem: Other things remaining the same, what happens in the market for air travel when consumers' incomes rise?
items.answer: Demand curve shifts to the right (increase in demand)
items.markingKey: (b) Demand curve shifts to the right (increase in demand).
options: Movement down along the demand curve (quantity demanded rises)
Demand curve shifts to the right (increase in demand)
Demand curve shifts to the left (decrease in demand)
Movement up along the demand curve (quantity demanded falls)

items.stem: Other things remaining the same, what happens in the market for tea when the price of coffee falls?
items.answer: Demand curve shifts to the left (decrease in demand)
items.markingKey: (a) Demand curve shifts to the left (decrease in demand).
options: Demand curve shifts to the left (decrease in demand)
Movement up along the demand curve (quantity demanded falls)
Movement down along the demand curve (quantity demanded rises)
Demand curve shifts to the right (increase in demand)

items.stem: When the price of fruits falls from ₹20 to ₹15, its quantity demanded rises from 500 to 550 units. Calculate the price elasticity of demand (absolute value) by the percentage method and state whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
items.answer: 0.4 (inelastic)

items.stem: When the price of tea changes from ₹40 to ₹35, quantity demanded changes from 150 to 181 units. Using the total expenditure method, the demand is
items.answer: Elastic (|eD| > 1)
items.markingKey: (b) Expenditure: ₹6,000 → ₹6,335; it moves opposite to price → elastic.

items.stem:
In a market, the demand for kites is q = 300 − 4p.
(i) Find the quantity demanded at ₹20 and ₹30.
(ii) Calculate the price elasticity of demand (absolute value) when price rises from ₹20 to ₹30, by the percentage method.
(iii) Is demand elastic, inelastic or unitary elastic over this range?
(iv) Find the total expenditure on kites at both prices.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each (4 marks).

items.stem: Why does a demand curve slope downward? Give two reasons.
items.answer: Substitution effect: good becomes relatively cheaper; income effect: real income rises; also law of DMU.
items.markingKey: 1½ marks each.

items.stem:
The demand for candles is q = 300 − 4p.
(i) Find the quantity demanded at ₹10 and ₹15.
(ii) Using the percentage method, find |eD| when price rises from ₹10 to ₹15.
(iii) Find the point elasticity at ₹10 using |e| = b × p/q.
(iv) Find total expenditure at both prices and state how it changes.
(v) At what price is the demand unitary elastic?
items.answer: (i) 260 and 240 units; (ii) (20/260) ÷ (5/10) = 0.15 (inelastic); (iii) 4 × 10/260 = 0.15; (iv) ₹2,600 and ₹3,600; expenditure rises; (v) p = 300/8 = 37.5 (mid-point of the demand line)
items.markingKey: 1 mark (i); 1½ marks (ii); 1 mark (iii); 1½ marks (iv); 1 mark (v) (6 marks).

items.stem: Other things remaining the same, what happens in the market for bread when the price of butter rises?
items.answer: Demand curve shifts to the left (decrease in demand)
items.markingKey: (a) Demand curve shifts to the left (decrease in demand).
options: Demand curve shifts to the left (decrease in demand)
Movement up along the demand curve (quantity demanded falls)
Demand curve shifts to the right (increase in demand)
Movement down along the demand curve (quantity demanded rises)

items.stem: Explain the percentage and geometric methods of measuring price elasticity of demand. Show on a straight-line demand curve where demand is elastic, unitary and inelastic.
items.answer: Percentage: eD = %ΔQ/%ΔP. Geometric: lower segment/upper segment at a point; mid-point e = 1, above mid-point e > 1, below e < 1, e = ∞ at price axis, 0 at quantity axis.
items.markingKey: 2 marks percentage; 2 marks geometric; 2 marks diagram (6 marks).

items.stem: A good may be normal for a consumer at low incomes and
items.answer: inferior at high incomes
items.markingKey: (a) NCERT: depends on income level.
options: a Giffen good at all incomes

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Demand for an inferior good falls as income rises.
Reason (R): Consumers switch to better-quality goods as their income rises.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Which pair of goods are substitutes?
items.answer: Train travel and bus travel
items.markingKey: (a) Train travel and bus travel: Substitutes. The others: Salt and televisions: Unrelated goods; Shoes and newspapers: Unrelated goods; Mobile phones and mobile data: Complements.

items.stem: When a household's monthly income changes from ₹40,000 to ₹25,000, its demand for Good X changes from 8 to 9 units per month (prices unchanged). Good X is a
items.answer: Inferior good
items.markingKey: (c) Demand moves opposite to income → inferior good.

items.stem: When the price of good Y changes from ₹50 to ₹55, the demand for good X changes from 41 to 51 units (price of X unchanged). X and Y are
items.answer: Substitutes
items.markingKey: (d) Demand for X moves with the price of Y → substitutes.

items.stem: Two consumers have demand curves q₁ = 80 − 2p and q₂ = 30 − 2p. Find the market demand at p = ₹1 and write the market demand function for prices at which both buy.
items.answer: 106 units; q = 110 − 4p
items.markingKey: q₁ = 78, q₂ = 28; total 106; adding the functions: q = (80 + 30) − (2 + 2)p.

items.stem: Goods that are used together, like cars and petrol, are
items.answer: complementary goods
items.markingKey: (b) Jointly demanded.

items.stem: Which pair of goods are complements?
items.answer: Cars and petrol
items.markingKey: (b) Cars and petrol: Complements. The others: Bicycles and table salt: Unrelated goods; Rice and wheat: Substitutes; Gel pens and ball pens: Substitutes.

items.stem: In the cardinal utility approach, utility is measured in
items.answer: utils
items.markingKey: (c) Cardinal measure.

items.stem:
Consider the markets for cotton shirts, polyester shirts, tea and sugar.
(i) How are cotton shirts and polyester shirts related?
(ii) What happens to the demand curve for cotton shirts if the price of polyester shirts rises?
(iii) How are tea and sugar related?
(iv) What happens to the demand curve for tea if the price of sugar rises?
items.answer: (i) Substitutes; (ii) Shifts to the right (demand increases); (iii) Complements; (iv) Shifts to the left (demand decreases)
items.markingKey: 1 mark each (4 marks).

items.stem: If the price of good 1 (on the x-axis) falls, the budget line
items.answer: becomes flatter, rotating outward along the x-axis
items.markingKey: (a) Slope −p₁/p₂ falls in size.
options: becomes flatter, rotating outward along the x-axis

items.stem: The price elasticity of demand for air travel is (−)0.5. At a price of ₹40, 1000 units are demanded. How many units will be demanded if the price falls to ₹32?
items.answer: 1100 units

items.stem:
Assertion (A): MU can become negative.
Reason (R): Consuming beyond the point of satiety reduces total utility.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Two indifference curves can never
items.answer: intersect each other
items.markingKey: (d) Intersection contradicts monotonicity.

items.stem: The demand function for kites is q = 200 − 5p. Find the price elasticity of demand (absolute value) at p = ₹36.
Two consumers have demand curves q₁ = 100 − 4p and q₂ = 40 − 3p. Find the market demand at p = ₹11 and write the market demand function for prices at which both buy.
items.answer: 63 units; q = 140 − 7p
items.markingKey: q₁ = 56, q₂ = 7; total 63; adding the functions: q = (100 + 40) − (4 + 3)p.

items.stem: A consumer has monotonic preferences. Compare bundle P = (4, 1) with bundle Q = (3, 2) (units of good 1, good 2).
items.answer: Cannot be decided from monotonic preferences alone
items.markingKey: (a) Neither bundle has at least as much of both goods with more of one.
options: Cannot be decided from monotonic preferences alone
The consumer is indifferent between them

items.stem: A consumer has ₹8. Good 1 costs ₹5 and good 2 costs ₹2; both are available only in whole units. How many bundles are in the budget set (affordable)?
Along a straight-line demand curve, price elasticity at the mid-point is
items.markingKey: (b) Lower = upper segment.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Elasticity is different at different points on a straight-line demand curve.
Reason (R): The slope is constant but the ratio p/q changes along the line.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem:
A consumer spends ₹45 on goods X and Y. Price of X = ₹6, price of Y = ₹3. Marginal utilities (utils) are:
Units | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
MU of X | 30 | 29 | 28 | 23 | 18 | 15
MU of Y | 25 | 21 | 16 | 13 | 9 | 7
Find the equilibrium combination using the law of equi-marginal utility.
items.answer: 5 units of X and 5 units of Y
items.markingKey: MUx/Px = 18/6 = 3 = MUy/Py = 9/3; spending = 6×5 + 3×5 = ₹45 = income. 2 marks ratios; 1 mark budget check; 1 mark answer.

items.stem:
Individual demand schedules of consumers in a market:
Price (₹) | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25
Demand of B | 36 | 27 | 22 | 17 | 8
Demand of A | 39 | 34 | 20 | 17 | 3
Demand of D | 39 | 31 | 29 | 7 | 3
Find the market demand at a price of ₹5.
items.answer: 114 units
items.markingKey: Market demand = horizontal sum = 36 + 39 + 39 = 114.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): At the optimum, MRS equals the price ratio.
Reason (R): If MRS > p₁/p₂, the consumer can gain by buying more of good 1.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R shows why any other point is not optimal.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A straight-line demand curve meets the price axis at ₹60. Using the geometric method, find the price elasticity of demand (absolute value) at a price of ₹4.
items.markingKey: |e| = lower segment/upper segment = p/(P₀ − p) = 4/(60 − 4) = 0.07. Below the mid-point demand is inelastic.

items.stem: Why is the budget line downward sloping? What does its slope show?
items.answer: Given income, more of one good means less of the other; slope −p₁/p₂ shows the rate at which good 2 can be exchanged for good 1 in the market.
items.markingKey: 1½ marks each.

items.stem: Market demand is obtained by
items.answer: horizontal summation of individual demand curves
items.markingKey: (b) Add quantities at each price.
options: vertical summation of individual demand curves
horizontal summation of individual demand curves

items.stem: A consumer has an income of ₹140 to spend on mangoes (good 1, price ₹20) and oranges (good 2, price ₹10). What is the maximum quantity of oranges the consumer can buy?
items.markingKey: Intercept = M/p = 140/10 = 14 (spending all income on oranges).

items.stem: At a bundle on her budget line, a consumer's MRS (units of good 2 she is willing to give up for one more unit of good 1) is 1.7. The prices are p₁ = ₹6 and p₂ = ₹5. What should she do to raise her satisfaction?
items.answer: Buy more of good 1 and less of good 2
items.markingKey: (b) MRS = 1.7 > p₁/p₂ = 1.2. She values good 1 more than the market does, so she substitutes good 1 for good 2.
options: Stay at the same bundle: it is the optimum
Buy more of good 1 and less of good 2
Buy less of good 1 and more of good 2

items.stem: Total utility is the
items.answer: sum of the marginal utilities of all units consumed
items.markingKey: (d) TU = ΣMU.
options: sum of the marginal utilities of all units consumed

items.stem:
Consider the markets for gel pens, ball pens, cars and petrol.
(i) How are gel pens and ball pens related?
(ii) What happens to the demand curve for gel pens if the price of ball pens rises?
(iii) How are cars and petrol related?
(iv) What happens to the demand curve for cars if the price of petrol rises?
items.answer: (i) Substitutes; (ii) Shifts to the right (demand increases); (iii) Complements; (iv) Shifts to the left (demand decreases)
items.markingKey: 1 mark each (4 marks).

items.stem: The budget line is a straight line because
items.answer: the prices of goods are given and constant
items.markingKey: (c) Constant price ratio.
options: the prices of goods are given and constant

items.stem: The price elasticity of demand for cars is (−)1. At a price of ₹10, 500 units are demanded. How many units will be demanded if the price rises to ₹12?
items.answer: 400 units

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A consumer buys more of a good when its price falls.
Reason (R): At a lower price, more units have MU in rupees at least equal to the price.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Preferences are monotonic when a consumer
items.answer: prefers a bundle with more of at least one good and no less of the other
items.markingKey: (d) More is preferred.
options: prefers a bundle with more of at least one good and no less of the other

items.stem: The demand function for kites is q = 120 − 10p. At what price is the demand unitary elastic?
items.markingKey: |e| = bp/q = 1 ⇒ 10p = 120 − 10p ⇒ p = 120/20 = 6 (mid-point of the demand line).

items.stem: Two consumers have demand curves q₁ = 60 − 2p and q₂ = 40 − 2p. Find the market demand at p = ₹9 and write the market demand function for prices at which both buy.
items.answer: 64 units; q = 100 − 4p
items.markingKey: q₁ = 42, q₂ = 22; total 64; adding the functions: q = (60 + 40) − (2 + 2)p.

items.stem: A consumer has monotonic preferences. Compare bundle P = (5, 7) with bundle Q = (7, 7) (units of good 1, good 2).
items.answer: Bundle Q is preferred
items.markingKey: (b) It has more of at least one good and no less of the other.
options: The consumer is indifferent between them
Cannot be decided from monotonic preferences alone

items.stem: A consumer has ₹15. Good 1 costs ₹5 and good 2 costs ₹5; both are available only in whole units. How many bundles lie on the budget line?
items.markingKey: Count (x₁, x₂) with 5x₁ + 5x₂ = 15: (0,3), (1,2), (2,1), (3,0) → 4 bundles.

items.stem: Demand for necessities such as salt tends to be
items.answer: inelastic
items.markingKey: (c) Needed whatever the price.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A rise in consumers' income shifts the demand curve for an inferior good to the right.
Reason (R): Consumers buy less of an inferior good when their income rises.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false: it shifts left. R is true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem:
A consumer spends ₹21 on goods X and Y. Price of X = ₹2, price of Y = ₹5. Marginal utilities (utils) are:
Units | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
MU of X | 14 | 9 | 6 | 4 | 3 | 1
MU of Y | 21 | 17 | 15 | 13 | 10 | 8
Find the equilibrium combination using the law of equi-marginal utility.
items.answer: 3 units of X and 3 units of Y
items.markingKey: MUx/Px = 6/2 = 3 = MUy/Py = 15/5; spending = 2×3 + 5×3 = ₹21 = income. 2 marks ratios; 1 mark budget check; 1 mark answer.

items.stem:
Individual demand schedules of consumers in a market:
Price (₹) | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50
Demand of C | 34 | 31 | 24 | 14 | 6
Demand of B | 34 | 33 | 29 | 24 | 11
Demand of D | 39 | 34 | 17 | 10 | 9
Find the market demand at a price of ₹50.
items.answer: 26 units
items.markingKey: Market demand = horizontal sum = 6 + 11 + 9 = 26.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A higher indifference curve gives lower satisfaction.
Reason (R): Bundles on a higher IC contain more of at least one good.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false; R is true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A straight-line demand curve meets the price axis at ₹40. Using the geometric method, find the price elasticity of demand (absolute value) at a price of ₹36.
items.markingKey: |e| = lower segment/upper segment = p/(P₀ − p) = 36/(40 − 36) = 9. Above the mid-point demand is elastic.

items.stem: Explain with a diagram the effect on the budget line of a fall in the price of good 1.
items.answer: The line rotates outward along the good 1 axis (intercept M/p₁ rises), good 2 intercept unchanged; it becomes flatter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark diagram; 2 marks explanation.

items.stem: Goods that can be used in place of each other are
items.answer: substitute goods
items.markingKey: (c) Substitutes.

items.stem: A consumer has an income of ₹4 to spend on notebooks (good 1, price ₹2) and pencils (good 2, price ₹2). What is the slope of the budget line (good 1 on the horizontal axis)?
items.markingKey: Slope = −p₁/p₂ = −2/2 = −1.

items.stem: At a bundle on her budget line, a consumer's MRS (units of good 2 she is willing to give up for one more unit of good 1) is 1.62. The prices are p₁ = ₹5 and p₂ = ₹8. What should she do to raise her satisfaction?
items.answer: Buy more of good 1 and less of good 2
items.markingKey: (b) MRS = 1.62 > p₁/p₂ = 0.62. She values good 1 more than the market does, so she substitutes good 1 for good 2.
options: Stay at the same bundle: it is the optimum
Buy more of good 1 and less of good 2
Buy less of good 1 and more of good 2
